meta.note: Song-misattribution backlog for /who-recorded/. Candidates: a cover mistaken for the ORIGINAL recording. Harvested 2026-07-22 (Wikipedia-verified), deduped; second harvest 2026-07-22 added 63 candidates across six veins (blues/British-invasion, soul-Motown, country-folk, reggae-ska, film-TV sync, standards & foreign-language). Tainted Love is already BUILT (data/songs/) — not listed. Build high-confusion first. Each becomes a data/songs/{songSlug}.json record modeled on tainted-love.json.

songs.title: Hound Dog
songs.whyNotable: Elvis's 1956 smash so dominated memory that most never encounter Big Mama Thornton's 1952 R&B original.

songs.title: Blue Suede Shoes
songs.whyNotable: Carl Perkins wrote AND first recorded it; Elvis's fame led the public to assume it was his.

songs.title: Suspicious Minds
songs.whyNotable: Mark James's 1968 original flopped uncharted; Elvis's 1969 comeback smash is universally taken as the original.

songs.title: Louie Louie
songs.whyNotable: The Kingsmen's 1963 garage-rock hit buried Richard Berry's 1957 original, a B-side he wrote and first recorded.

songs.title: Twist and Shout
songs.whyNotable: The Beatles' 1963 recording is so theirs that few know the Top Notes cut it first in 1961 (the Isley Brothers 1962 is also earlier).

songs.title: Respect
songs.whyNotable: Aretha's 1967 reworking became so definitive the public rarely knows Otis Redding wrote and first recorded it in 1965.

songs.title: Piece of My Heart
songs.whyNotable: Joplin's 1968 Big Brother version buried Erma Franklin's 1967 soul original.

songs.title: Me and Bobby McGee
songs.whyNotable: Joplin's posthumous 1971 No. 1 is so hers that few know Roger Miller recorded it first in 1969.

songs.title: Black Magic Woman
songs.whyNotable: Peter Green wrote and recorded it for early Fleetwood Mac in 1968; Santana's 1970 version is the one everyone thinks is original.

songs.title: Red Red Wine
songs.whyNotable: UB40 themselves didn't know Neil Diamond wrote it (1967); their 1983 reggae version is taken as the original.

songs.title: Blinded by the Light
songs.whyNotable: Manfred Mann's Earth Band took it to No. 1 (1977); it's remembered as theirs, not Springsteen's 1973 original.

songs.title: Nothing Compares 2 U
songs.whyNotable: Prince wrote it and his side project The Family recorded it first (1985, no single); O'Connor's 1990 hit is taken as the original.

songs.title: Girls Just Want to Have Fun
songs.whyNotable: Robert Hazard wrote and demoed it in 1979 as a male-perspective song; almost no one knows a man recorded it first.

songs.title: Torn
songs.writer: Scott Cutler, Anne Preven, Phil Thornalley
songs.whyNotable: Written 1991; first RELEASED as the Danish 'Brændt' by Lis Sørensen (1993), then in English by Ednaswap (1995); Imbruglia's 1997 hit is assumed original — many think she wrote it.

songs.title: I Love Rock 'n' Roll
songs.whyNotable: British band Arrows recorded it first (1975); Jett's 1982 chart-topper is assumed to be the source.

songs.title: Hurt
songs.whyNotable: Reznor wrote and recorded it for NIN (1994); Cash's 2003 version is so definitive Reznor said 'that song isn't mine anymore.'

songs.title: Valerie
songs.whyNotable: The 2007 Ronson/Winehouse soul version so eclipsed the Liverpool indie band's 2006 original that most assume it's a Winehouse song.

songs.title: Girl You Know It's True
songs.whyNotable: Written and first recorded by the little-known Maryland group Numarx earlier the same year Milli Vanilli's global hit landed.

songs.title: Killing Me Softly with His Song
songs.whyNotable: Lori Lieberman recorded it first (1972), Roberta Flack made it a 1973 standard; a generation knows only the Fugees' 1996 version.

songs.title: I Will Always Love You
songs.whyNotable: Parton wrote and first recorded it (1973-74); Houston's 1992 Bodyguard version leads many to assume it was written for her.

songs.title: Mad World
songs.whyNotable: The stark 2003 Jules/Andrews piano version leads many younger listeners to think it's the original, not a slowed reworking of a 1982 Tears for Fears hit.

songs.title: Higher Ground
songs.whyNotable: Stevie Wonder's 1973 Innervisions classic is well known, but many rock-era listeners assume the 1989 RHCP version originated it.
songs.dropReason: No documentable public belief RHCP originated it; Stevie Wonder original is a #4 pop/#1 R&B hit, RHCP version widely known AS a cover.

songs.title: The Man Who Sold the World
songs.whyNotable: Bowie's 1970 original is a deep cut; after Nirvana's 1993 Unplugged version many younger fans credited the song to Nirvana.

songs.title: Hallelujah
songs.whyNotable: Cohen's authorship is fairly well known, but Buckley's 1994 version is so dominant many believe his recording is the original.

songs.title: Feeling Good
songs.whyNotable: Written for the 1964 musical 'The Roar of the Greasepaint' and first performed by Cy Grant; assumed to originate with Simone's 1965 (or Bublé's 2005) version.

songs.title: Fever
songs.whyNotable: Peggy Lee's 1958 rearrangement became her signature, overshadowing Little Willie John's 1956 R&B original.

songs.title: Cups (When I'm Gone)
songs.writer: A.P. Carter (1931 song); cup arrangement by Heloise Tunstall-Behrens and Luisa Gerstein
songs.whyNotable: Kendrick's Pitch Perfect version is assumed original, but the viral cup arrangement was created by Lulu and the Lampshades (2009) atop A.P. Carter's 1931 folk song.

songs.title: Dazed and Confused
songs.whyNotable: Holmes wrote and recorded it for his 1967 debut album; Led Zeppelin's 1969 debut credited it to Jimmy Page alone. Holmes sued Page in 2010, the case was dismissed with prejudice in January 2012 after a settlement, and later releases changed the credit to 'By Page - Inspired by Jake Holmes'.

songs.title: When the Levee Breaks
songs.originalArtist: Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie
songs.writer: Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie
songs.whyNotable: One of the most sampled drum tracks in music history is a 1971 rearrangement of a Delta blues record cut in June 1929. Zeppelin's version credits Memphis Minnie alongside the band; McCoy, whom Charles Shaar Murray identifies as the actual songwriter, is not on the Zeppelin credit.

songs.title: Bring It On Home
songs.whyNotable: Recorded by Sonny Boy Williamson II on 11 January 1963 for Checker and released in 1966. Zeppelin's Led Zeppelin II track opened and closed with deliberate quotations of it; Chess publisher Arc Music sued, the band settled, and later reissues give Willie Dixon sole songwriting credit.

songs.title: Babe I'm Gonna Leave You
songs.whyNotable: Written by Anne Bredon in the late 1950s; the first published recording was Joan Baez's 1962 in-concert album, credited there only as traditional. Zeppelin's 1969 debut credited it 'Traditional, arr. Jimmy Page' until Bredon approached the band and won credit plus back royalties in 1990.

songs.title: The House of the Rising Sun
songs.whyNotable: The oldest known recording is the Appalachian duo Ashley and Foster's, cut 6 September 1933 for Vocalion. Guthrie, Lead Belly, Josh White, Baez, Simone and Dylan all recorded it before the Animals' June 1964 single, which the public treats as the song's point of origin.

songs.title: The Train Kept A-Rollin'
songs.writer: Tiny Bradshaw, Lois Mann and Howard Kay
songs.whyNotable: A classic-rock staple most listeners file under Aerosmith began as a jump-blues record cut by bandleader Tiny Bradshaw in Cincinnati on 6 October 1951. 'Lois Mann' is a pseudonym of King Records owner Syd Nathan, added so the label boss could collect publishing royalties.

songs.title: Rollin' and Tumblin'
songs.whyNotable: Even blues listeners name Muddy Waters, who cut it in 1950, but the first recording was made in Atlanta on 14 March 1929 by the near-forgotten Hambone Willie Newbern for Okeh. Cream's 1966 Fresh Cream version added a third layer for rock audiences.

songs.title: Baby, Please Don't Go
songs.writer: Traditional (Joe Williams credited on the record)
songs.whyNotable: Big Joe Williams cut it in Chicago on 31 October 1935, billed as Joe Williams' Washboard Blues Singers. Them's October 1964 Decca recording with the 19-year-old Van Morrison is now treated as definitive, and AC/DC's 1975 version added another layer.

songs.title: Need Your Love So Bad
songs.writer: Mertis John Jr. and William Edward John
songs.whyNotable: Little Willie John released it on King on 20 October 1955 and it reached No. 5 on the Billboard R&B chart in 1956. Peter Green's string-laden Blue Horizon single from July 1968 is the version British audiences know, and it is routinely assumed to be a Fleetwood Mac original.

songs.title: Mustang Sally
songs.whyNotable: Mack Rice wrote it and cut it himself as 'Sir Mack Rice' for Blue Rock in May 1965; Pickett's 1966 Atlantic version buried it so completely that the song is now treated as a Pickett original.

songs.title: Land of 1000 Dances
songs.whyNotable: New Orleans R&B singer Chris Kenner wrote and first recorded it on Instant in 1962; Pickett's 1966 Atlantic cut (No. 6 pop, No. 1 R&B) is the best-known version and is widely assumed to be the original. The famous chanted hook belongs to neither - Cannibal & the Headhunters added it on their 1965 Rampart version.

songs.title: If You Don't Know Me by Now
songs.whyNotable: A Philly soul landmark sung by Teddy Pendergrass (No. 1 R&B, No. 3 pop, 1972) that a generation now hears as a Simply Red song after Mick Hucknall's 1989 US No. 1. Gamble and Huff originally wrote it for Labelle, who never recorded it.

songs.title: Money (That's What I Want)
songs.whyNotable: Barrett Strong's 1959 Tamla single became Motown's first hit in June 1960; the Beatles' 1963 closer on With the Beatles is the version most listeners meet first. The Rolling Stones cut it too, in January 1964.

songs.title: Cry Baby
songs.whyNotable: Garnet Mimms took it to No. 1 R&B and No. 4 pop in 1963, but Joplin's posthumous Pearl version is so identified with her that Mimms has largely vanished from the song's story.

songs.title: Papa Was a Rollin' Stone
songs.whyNotable: Whitfield gave it to the Undisputed Truth first - single released 9 May 1972 on Gordy, a modest No. 63 pop - then re-cut it with the Temptations four months later for a Hot 100 No. 1 and three Grammys. Same label, same producer, and the first version is almost entirely forgotten.

songs.title: War
songs.whyNotable: The Temptations recorded it first, on the March 1970 album Psychedelic Shack, but Motown refused to release it as their single for fear of the group's image - so Whitfield re-recorded it with Edwin Starr, whose June 1970 Gordy single went to No. 1.

songs.title: Some Kind of Wonderful
songs.whyNotable: John Ellison wrote it and cut it with his own R&B group Soul Brothers Six for Atlantic in 1967, where it stalled at No. 91. Grand Funk's December 1974 Capitol single hit No. 3, and the song is now heard as a rock original rather than a failed soul 45.

songs.title: It's All Over Now
songs.whyNotable: Bobby Womack's group the Valentinos recorded it on 24 March 1964 for Sam Cooke's SAR label and reached only No. 94; the Stones cut theirs at Chess Studios on 10 June, releasing it on 26 June for their first UK No. 1. Barely three months separate the original from the version that erased it.

songs.title: Everybody Needs Somebody to Love
songs.writer: Bert Berns, Solomon Burke and Jerry Wexler
songs.whyNotable: Solomon Burke co-wrote and recorded it on 28 May 1964, released that July on Atlantic; the 1980 Blues Brothers film performance is now the default reference point for a whole generation. The Rolling Stones had already covered it in January 1965.

songs.title: The First Cut Is the Deepest
songs.whyNotable: Soul singer P. P. Arnold released the first recording on 21 April 1967 on Immediate, months before writer Cat Stevens issued his own version on New Masters (15 December 1967). Rod Stewart's 1977 hit and Sheryl Crow's 2003 version are what most listeners know, and the song's first voice was neither.

songs.title: Take Me to the River
songs.whyNotable: Al Green co-wrote and first recorded it on Al Green Explores Your Mind in 1974, but Hi Records never issued his version as a single - it released Syl Johnson's 1975 cover instead. Talking Heads' 1978 Sire single reached No. 26 and is often taken for the source.

songs.title: Time Is on My Side
songs.writer: Jerry Ragovoy (as 'Norman Meade'), with lyrics by Jimmy Norman
songs.whyNotable: The Stones' first US top ten is a cover twice over: Irma Thomas cut it in April 1964, but the first recording was jazz trombonist Kai Winding's, released on Verve in October 1963. The verse lyrics everyone knows were written by session singer Jimmy Norman at the Thomas session.

songs.title: Wagon Wheel
songs.whyNotable: Old Crow Medicine Show's string-band version, released 10 February 2004, spread by word of mouth and never charted mainstream; Rucker's 2013 Capitol single hit No. 1 country and went 11x platinum. The chorus itself is an unfinished 1973 Dylan sketch that Secor built verses around.

songs.title: Seven Bridges Road
songs.whyNotable: Country-folk songwriter Steve Young wrote and first recorded it for his 1969 A&M album Rock Salt & Nails; the Eagles' harmony live version, recorded 28 July 1980 and issued as a single that December, reached No. 21 and is now assumed to be an Eagles original.

songs.title: Love Hurts
songs.whyNotable: The Everly Brothers cut it first in July 1960 and buried it as an album track on A Date with the Everly Brothers - never a single. Nazareth's 1974 power-ballad rendition is the only version ever to be a US hit single, which is why the song reads as a Scottish hard-rock original.

songs.title: Rhinestone Cowboy
songs.whyNotable: Writer Larry Weiss recorded it himself on his 1974 album Black and Blue Suite, where it made no commercial impact outside a No. 71 placing in Australia; Campbell's May 1975 version topped both the Hot 100 and the country chart and became his signature song.

songs.title: Delta Dawn
songs.whyNotable: Co-writer Alex Harvey recorded it first, on his November 1971 Capitol album; Tanya Tucker's April 1972 Columbia country hit came next, and Helen Reddy's June 1973 pop version - a US No. 1 - is the one most people name.

songs.title: Tennessee Waltz
songs.originalArtist: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys
songs.writer: Pee Wee King and Redd Stewart
songs.whyNotable: Pee Wee King's band recorded it 2 December 1947 and RCA Victor released it in January 1948, a No. 3 country hit; Patti Page's November 1950 Mercury pop version spent nine weeks at No. 1 and eclipsed the country original entirely.

songs.title: Turn! Turn! Turn!
songs.whyNotable: Seeger wrote it in 1959, but the first released recording was the Limeliters' 'To Everything There Is a Season' on their 1962 RCA Victor album Folk Matinee, ahead of Seeger's own version that same year; the Byrds' October 1965 Columbia single went to No. 1 and owns the song publicly.

songs.title: Mr. Bojangles
songs.whyNotable: Walker wrote it about a street performer he met in a New Orleans jail and cut it at Phillips Recording in Memphis, released by Atco on 20 June 1968; the Dirt Band's 1970 recording became a No. 9 hit in 1971, and Sammy Davis Jr.'s 1972 showpiece muddies the attribution further.

songs.title: You Are My Sunshine
songs.writer: Credited to Jimmie Davis and Charles Mitchell (authorship disputed)
songs.whyNotable: The Pine Ridge Boys recorded it 22 August 1939 and Bluebird released it 6 October 1939, with no songwriter listed; the Rice Brothers' Gang cut it for Decca on 13 September 1939. Davis did not record it until 5 February 1940, after buying the rights from Paul Rice - yet he is universally treated as both author and first recorder.

songs.title: The Tide Is High
songs.whyNotable: Blondie's 1980 US and UK No. 1 is routinely treated as a Blondie song, but it is a cover of a 1967 Jamaican rocksteady single by The Paragons, written by their lead singer John Holt and cut for Duke Reid's Treasure Isle.

songs.title: Rivers of Babylon
songs.whyNotable: One of the best-selling UK singles ever and universally filed as Euro-disco by Boney M., yet it was written and recorded in 1970 by Jamaican rocksteady group The Melodians for Leslie Kong, and reached the world via The Harder They Come.

songs.title: A Message to You, Rudy
songs.whyNotable: The 2 Tone anthem is assumed to be a Specials original, but Dandy Livingstone wrote and recorded it in London in 1967; Rico Rodriguez played the trombone intro on both his version and the Specials' 1979 remake.

songs.title: Kingston Town
songs.whyNotable: UB40's signature ballad, a UK No. 4 and a No. 1 in France and the Netherlands, is a cover of Lord Creator's 1970 Clandisc single produced by Clancy Eccles - the same Labour of Love covers-project trap as their Red Red Wine.

songs.title: Pass the Dutchie
songs.writer: The Mighty Diamonds (adapted from Leroy Sibbles' 1968 instrumental 'Full Up')
songs.whyNotable: Musical Youth's 1982 UK No. 1 is remembered as a novelty original, but it is a sanitised retitling of The Mighty Diamonds' 1981 'Pass the Kouchie'; a 2012 High Court case confirmed the two share the same copyright.

songs.title: Monkey Man
songs.whyNotable: A staple of the Specials' 1979 debut and widely taken for a 2 Tone original, it is Toots Hibbert's 1969 Leslie Kong-produced single, a modest UK No. 47 whose British fame arrived a decade later.

songs.title: I Can See Clearly Now
songs.whyNotable: The reverse-direction trap: because Jimmy Cliff's Cool Runnings version is the one a generation grew up with, the song is often taken for a Jamaican reggae standard, when it was written and recorded by American singer Johnny Nash and was a US No. 1 in 1972.

songs.title: Don't Turn Around
songs.whyNotable: Twice mistaken: Ace of Base's 1994 hit is usually taken as theirs, and those who know better usually credit Aswad's 1988 UK No. 1 reggae version - but the first recording was Tina Turner's, issued in 1986 as the B-side of 'Typical Male'.

songs.title: Everything I Own
songs.whyNotable: In Britain the song reads as a reggae standard thanks to Ken Boothe's 1974 UK No. 1 and Boy George's 1987 number one, but David Gates wrote it for Bread as an elegy for his father and their version charted in the US in 1972.

songs.title: Everybody's Talkin'
songs.whyNotable: The textbook sync case: Nilsson's 1968 recording flopped as a single, then Midnight Cowboy made it a hit so total that the song is now subtitled 'Theme from Midnight Cowboy'. Fred Neil wrote and recorded it first, on his self-titled Capitol album released December 1966.

songs.title: Unchained Melody
songs.whyNotable: Written for the 1955 prison film Unchained and first recorded by Todd Duncan for that film. The Righteous Brothers cut their version in March 1965 for Philles, originally a B-side, and the 1990 film Ghost made that recording the version an entire generation met first - and assumes is the original.

songs.title: Hooked on a Feeling
songs.whyNotable: B. J. Thomas recorded it first, released October 1968 on Scepter. Blue Swede's 1974 cover bolted on a chanted intro borrowed from a 1971 Jonathan King version, and Reservoir Dogs plus the Guardians of the Galaxy trailers made that arrangement the only one most listeners have ever heard.

songs.title: You Got the Love
songs.writer: Anthony B. Stephens, Arnecia Michelle Harris and John Bellamy
songs.whyNotable: A pure TV-sync case. The Source featuring Candi Staton released it in 1986; Florence + the Machine's 2009 Island version was carried into mass awareness by the Gossip Girl and Gavin & Stacey finales and Sky Sports football coverage, and a large cohort has never encountered the 1986 record at all.

songs.title: Make You Feel My Love
songs.whyNotable: Bob Dylan wrote it, but Billy Joel's recording (as 'To Make You Feel My Love', 13 August 1997) reached the public first, ahead of Dylan's own Time Out of Mind release on 30 September 1997. Adele's 2008 version, propelled by X Factor performances in 2010, is now widely assumed to be the song's origin.

songs.title: The Best
songs.whyNotable: Bonnie Tyler released it first, in January 1988 from her album Hide Your Heart. Tina Turner's August 1989 Capitol cover - which added a bridge and a key change at her request - became the version used across decades of advertising and is near-universally taken for the original.

songs.title: Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon
songs.whyNotable: Neil Diamond wrote and first recorded it, released March 1967 on Bang. Urge Overkill's version, cut for their 1992 EP Stull, became the definitive one for a generation after its use in Pulp Fiction - many viewers meet it as an Urge Overkill song with no idea a 1967 original exists.

songs.title: Bang Bang (My Baby Shot Me Down)
songs.whyNotable: Cher recorded it first, on 11 February 1966, released later that month on Imperial. Nancy Sinatra's cover from the same year was placed over the opening credits of Kill Bill: Volume 1, and post-Tarantino audiences overwhelmingly treat the Sinatra recording as the original.

songs.title: Try a Little Tenderness
songs.originalArtist: Ray Noble Orchestra (vocal by Val Rosing)
songs.writer: Harry M. Woods, Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly
songs.whyNotable: Published November 1932 and first recorded that December by the Ray Noble Orchestra. Otis Redding's 1966 Volt/Atco reading is so definitive that almost nobody knows it is a cover of a pre-war standard.

songs.title: Iko Iko
songs.originalArtist: James "Sugar Boy" Crawford and His Cane Cutters
songs.whyNotable: First recorded in November 1953 as 'Jock-A-Mo' by James 'Sugar Boy' Crawford on Checker. The Dixie Cups' March 1965 Red Bird version renamed it and is treated as the source; the Belle Stars' 1982 cover charted in the US only after Rain Man, adding a third generation of confusion.

songs.title: My Way
songs.writer: Jacques Revaux (music); Claude François and Gilles Thibaut (original French lyrics); Paul Anka (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: The definitive Sinatra signature song is an English rewrite of the French chanson 'Comme d'habitude', recorded and released by Claude François in November 1967. Paul Anka bought the adaptation rights after hearing the tune on French radio.

songs.title: Seasons in the Sun
songs.whyNotable: Brel recorded the French original 'Le Moribond' on 22 February 1961, released that July. The Kingston Trio cut the first English version in 1963 using Rod McKuen's adaptation; Terry Jacks recorded his own reworking in Vancouver in 1973.

songs.title: Sukiyaki
songs.whyNotable: Released in Japan on 15 October 1961 as 'Ue o Muite Arukō', Kyu Sakamoto's record was renamed 'Sukiyaki' abroad. A Taste of Honey's 1981 version used entirely new English words, and 4 P.M.'s 1994 hit copied that arrangement, leaving two generations who never met the Japanese original.

songs.title: The Lion Sleeps Tonight
songs.writer: Solomon Linda (original); George David Weiss (English adaptation)
songs.whyNotable: The a cappella Zulu record 'Mbube' was cut by Solomon Linda's group at Gallo's Johannesburg studio in 1939. It reached the West via Alan Lomax and The Weavers' 'Wimoweh' (1951) before The Tokens' RCA Victor single of October 1961 became the version the world credits - while Linda received essentially nothing.

songs.title: You Don't Have to Say You Love Me
songs.writer: Pino Donaggio and Vito Pallavicini (original); Vicki Wickham and Simon Napier-Bell (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: Donaggio debuted 'Io che non vivo (senza te)' at the 1965 Sanremo Festival and took it to No. 1 in Italy that March. Springfield, who heard it at Sanremo, taped her English version in London on 9-10 March 1966.

songs.title: Fly Me to the Moon
songs.whyNotable: Bart Howard wrote it in 1954 as 'In Other Words', and the first commercial recording was Kaye Ballard's, issued by Decca in April 1954 and reviewed in Billboard that May. Sinatra's Count Basie/Quincy Jones recording came a decade later, in 1964, and swallowed the song's identity whole.

songs.title: The Girl from Ipanema
songs.writer: Antônio Carlos Jobim (music); Vinícius de Moraes (Portuguese lyrics); Norman Gimbel (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: 'Garota de Ipanema' was written in 1962 and first commercially recorded that year by Brazilian singer Pery Ribeiro. The Getz/Gilberto recording everyone treats as the original was taped in March 1963 and released on Verve in March 1964.

songs.title: Sway
songs.originalArtist: Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta
songs.writer: Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz (original); Norman Gimbel (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: The Mexican bolero-mambo '¿Quién será?' was first recorded as an instrumental by Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta for RCA Victor in 1953. Dean Martin's Capitol single of 1954 carried Norman Gimbel's unrelated English lyric, and Michael Bublé's 2004 revival pushed the Spanish original further out of view.

songs.title: Beyond the Sea
songs.writer: Charles Trenet (French original 'La Mer'); Jack Lawrence (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: Trenet's 'La Mer' was published in 1946, but the first recording was made by Roland Gerbeau in December 1945, ahead of Trenet's own. Jack Lawrence's English lyric turned an ode to the sea into a love song; Darin's Atco single did not appear until January 1960.

songs.title: Both Sides, Now
songs.originalArtist: Dave Van Ronk and the Hudson Dusters
songs.whyNotable: Mitchell wrote it, but she was the third act to put it on record: Dave Van Ronk and the Hudson Dusters released it as 'Clouds' in June 1967 and Judy Collins cut it for Wildflowers the same year. Mitchell's own recording did not appear until the 1969 Reprise album Clouds.

songs.title: Mas que Nada
songs.whyNotable: Jorge Ben recorded his own song on his 1963 Philips debut Samba Esquema Novo. Mendes' 1966 Brasil '66 version is so dominant outside Brazil that it is widely treated as definitive.

songs.title: Let It Be Me
songs.writer: Gilbert Bécaud (music) and Pierre Delanoë (French lyrics); Manny Curtis (English lyrics)
songs.whyNotable: The song began as the French 'Je t'appartiens', sung by Bécaud and released as an HMV single in 1955. Jill Corey sang the first English version on television in 1957; the Everly Brothers recorded theirs in December 1959, and Cadence released it in 1960.

songs.title: What a Diff'rence a Day Makes
songs.whyNotable: María Grever's Spanish song 'Cuando vuelva a tu lado' was written and first recorded in 1934, by Orquesta Pedro Vía. Washington's 1959 Mercury single won a Grammy and is treated as the song's origin point, twenty-five years late.
